name: Transportation
blurb: Autonomous driving is the visible front; AI also runs freight matching, maritime navigation, transit, and aviation, from IMO and EASA to the trucking, shipping, and aviation majors.

points.desc: Waymo's safety hub, with its published methodology and crash-rate comparisons, is the most complete public evidence base from an AV operator.
points.name: Waymo publishes its safety record

points.desc: Vision-language-action and control models are tracked in the Robotics Models section.
points.name: Robotics models are catalogued on this site

points.desc: The International Maritime Organization's MASS work - Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships - is where international rules for AI navigation, collision avoidance, and crewless vessels are being written.
points.name: The IMO governs autonomous shipping

points.desc: The FAA's innovation work and EASA's AI roadmap are the regulatory record for AI flight systems, automated risk management, and eVTOL certification - nothing flies commercially without them.
points.name: FAA and EASA gate aviation AI

points.desc: The American Trucking Associations is the industry body tracking policy and adoption for autonomous freight and AI logistics.
points.name: ATA tracks autonomous trucking policy

points.desc: The pure-play autonomous trucking platforms operating Level 4 freight on commercial highway corridors - their own operations pages are the deployment record.
points.name: Aurora and Kodiak run the driverless corridors

points.desc: C.H. Robinson applies AI to load matching, dynamic pricing, and multi-modal route optimization at one of the largest freight networks.
points.name: Freight brokerage runs on prediction

points.desc: Wärtsilä's vessel-optimization and autonomous-navigation technology is the commercial maritime AI record; Maersk applies AI across global route and port-congestion prediction.
points.name: Maritime AI ships from the equipment makers

points.desc: Airbus's innovation programs and Boeing's autonomy work cover AI flight management and predictive maintenance for commercial aircraft.
points.name: Aviation incumbents test AI in the cockpit and the hangar

points.desc: Samsara's AI dashcams and sensor networks monitor driver behavior and predict maintenance across commercial fleets; Mobileye supplies the computer-vision stack in driver-assist systems worldwide.
points.name: Fleet telematics is deployed AI at scale

points.desc: The enterprise AI platform used by airlines and rail operators for fleet and crew optimization is a tracked company in the directory.
points.name: Palantir is tracked on this site

summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
About 11.2 percent of transportation and warehousing firms reported using AI in the latest survey period, up from 10.7 percent the prior period, suggesting slow but consistent adoption in a sector where the public conversation has long been dominated by autonomous vehicles. The gap between the headline drama of self-driving technology and the actual adoption numbers reflects how much of the sector remains operationally conservative, even as the infrastructure investment from major players accumulates. Waymo maintains the most complete public safety evidence base among autonomous vehicle operators, while Aurora and Kodiak are running Level 4 freight commercially on highway corridors, and C.H. Robinson applies AI to load matching, dynamic pricing, and route optimization across one of the largest freight networks in the world. Fleet telematics represents probably the most widely deployed AI in the sector today, with Samsara running AI dashcam and sensor networks across commercial fleets and Mobileye supplying computer-vision stacks in driver-assist systems at scale.

The money and vendor concentration split across three distinct layers. At the vehicle and vessel level, Wärtsilä handles vessel optimization and autonomous navigation in maritime, Maersk applies AI to route planning and port-congestion prediction, and Airbus and Boeing are both running AI programs in flight management and predictive maintenance. At the infrastructure and optimization layer, enterprise platforms including Palantir are used by airlines and rail operators for fleet and crew scheduling. The regulatory layer is equally concentrated: the FAA and EASA together control what can fly commercially, the International Maritime Organization's MASS program is writing the international rules for autonomous shipping including collision avoidance and crewless vessel standards, and the American Trucking Associations is the principal policy tracking body for autonomous freight.

The risks the record shows are primarily regulatory and liability-based rather than technological. Nothing flies commercially without FAA or EASA certification, and the IMO's MASS framework is still being written, meaning autonomous shipping at scale remains a regulatory work-in-progress regardless of what the hardware can do. Aviation AI certification timelines are long and the eVTOL category adds further complexity. In trucking the Level 4 corridor deployments are real but geographically limited, and policy coordination through bodies like the American Trucking Associations suggests the industry is still negotiating the liability and standards questions that would enable broader rollout.

A reader deciding whether to deploy should distinguish sharply between what is available now and what remains developmental. Fleet telematics, AI dashcams, predictive maintenance, and freight matching are mature enough to evaluate against straightforward operational metrics, and the vendor ecosystem for those applications is established. Autonomous vehicle and vessel programs require navigating certification regimes that operate on multi-year timescales and in some cases lack finalized rules entirely. The steady but modest rise in the adoption figures suggests that most firms are finding the incremental operational applications easier to act on than the transformative ones, which is probably the right read of where the evidence currently sits.
